subject: English
passage: In a series of field experiments, Daniel Colombo and John Colombo demonstrated that manipulating the amount of open space between understory shrubs can influence songbirds' selection of nest sites. Birds in several of the experiments settled on nest sites in the same (generic) woodland plots at significantly higher rates when the shrub-to-space ratio was low than when it was high. But in one of the experiments, the Colombos arranged the same shrub clusters with different amounts of intervening open space in a mature old-growth forest and in a recently logged secondary forest. The result of this experiment suggests that a habitat context associated with degraded, low-quality woodland may moderate the effect the Colombos observed in their other experiments.
prompt: Which finding from the experiment with the old-growth forest and the secondary forest, if true, would most directly support the conclusion presented in the text?

choices.A: In the old-growth forest, birds settled on nest sites with widely spaced shrubs at substantially higher rates than on nest sites with closely spaced shrubs, but in the secondary forest, birds settled on nest sites with widely spaced shrubs at only slightly higher rates than on nest sites with closely spaced shrubs.
choices.B: In both the old-growth forest and the secondary forest, birds settled on nest sites with widely spaced shrubs at lower rates than on nest sites with closely spaced shrubs, but the difference in settlement rates was significantly greater in the old-growth forest than in the secondary forest.
choices.C: Birds settled on nest sites with widely spaced shrubs in the old-growth forest at rates similar to those of nest sites with widely spaced shrubs in the secondary forest, but birds settled on nest sites with closely spaced shrubs in the old-growth forest at higher rates than on nest sites with closely spaced shrubs in the secondary forest.
choices.D: When shrubs were widely spaced, birds settled on nest sites in the old-growth forest at higher rates than on nest sites in the secondary forest, but when shrubs were closely spaced, birds settled on nest sites in the old-growth forest at lower rates than on nest sites in the secondary forest.

explanation:
Choice A is the best answer because it presents a finding that, if true, would support the text's conclusion about the experiment with the old-growth forest and the secondary forest. According to the text, the Colombos found in several experiments that when shrubs in a generic woodland plot are arranged with a low shrub-to-space ratio (that is, with lots of open space between them), birds settle on nest sites at significantly higher rates than when the same shrubs are arranged with a higher shrub-to-space ratio. The text then states that the results of an experiment specifically using the contexts of a degraded, low-quality forest (the secondary forest) and a high-quality forest (the old-growth forest) suggest that a low-quality habitat context may moderate, or lessen, that effect. If the Colombos found that birds in the experiment with the old-growth forest settled on nest sites at substantially higher rates when shrubs were widely spaced than when they were closely spaced, but birds in the secondary forest settled at only slightly higher rates under the same conditions, that finding would demonstrate that increased spacing between shrubs was associated with less of an increase in settlement rates in the low-quality forest than in the high-quality forest. Thus, the finding would support the text's conclusion that a low-quality habitat context moderates the effect the Colombos observed in their earlier experiments.

Why C is incorrect:

Choice C is incorrect because this finding wouldn't show that the effect the Colombos observed in their initial experiments (that nest sites with widely spaced shrubs are selected at higher rates than nest sites with closely spaced shrubs) is present but lessened in degraded habitats, as the text suggests. The conclusion in the text rests on determining the difference in settlement rates between the two spacing conditions within each forest and then comparing the difference for the low-quality forest to the difference for the high-quality forest; a finding that compares settlement rates between the two forests for only one type of spacing condition at a time wouldn't provide information about the degree of difference between spacing conditions within each type of habitat context.
